content: Boxthorn, scientifically known as Lycium, is a genus of plants belonging to the tribe Lycieae within the family Solanaceae. This genus comprises approximately 90 species of plants that are native to various subtropical regions across the globe. These plants are predominantly found in arid, semi-saline environments. Common names for Lycium species include wolfberry, desert-thorn, Christmas berry, and matrimony vine. The term tea-tree is also sometimes used, though misleadingly, as these plants are not related to tea and their foliage is toxic, making them unsuitable for use as tea. The name goji has become widely recognized in English, largely due to the popularity of American-produced juices and dried berries marketed as Tibetan or Himalayan goji berries. However, these geographical labels do not accurately reflect the true origins of the berries. The distribution of Lycium species is as follows: approximately 20 species are found in North America, 30 in South America, 30 in Africa, 10 in Eurasia, and one species in Australia. The genera Grabowskia and Phrodus are closely related to Lycium and are also part of the tribe Lycieae. Lycium plants are long-lived, perennial, thorny shrubs. They have deciduous, alternate, simple leaves that range from 1 to 8 cm in length. The flowers are either solitary or arranged in small clusters, measuring 6 to 25 mm in diameter. The corolla consists of five petals, which may be purple, white, or greenish-white, and are fused at their bases. The fruit is a fleshy, multi-seeded berry, 8 to 20 mm in diameter, and can be red, yellow, orange, purple, or black in color. These berries resemble those of nightshade and bittersweet plants. In some species, such as Lycium barbarum (commonly known as wolfberry), the fruit is edible. Most Lycium species are co-sexual, meaning their flowers possess both male and female reproductive structures. However, some species exhibit gender dimorphism, where male and female flowers are found on separate plants. Evidence suggests that sexual dimorphism has evolved multiple times within the Lycium genus. Certain species, such as Lycium californicum, have populations that are both monoecious (having male and female flowers on the same plant) and dioecious (having male and female flowers on separate plants). The medicinal properties of Lycium have been recognized since ancient times. European herbalists were familiar with the plant, and it was described by Pliny the Elder in his Naturalis Historia as a treatment for sore eyes and inflammation. Similarly, Pedanius Dioscorides mentioned Lycium in his work De Materia Medica. In 1753, Carl Linnaeus described three species of Lycium—L. afrum, L. barbarum, and L. europaeum—in his publication Species Plantarum. Uses The fruit, leaves, and bark of certain Lycium species have been utilized in China for over 2,000 years. The fruit, known in China as gouqizi (枸杞子) or wolfberry (Lycium barbarum), is commonly used in herbal teas, soups, juices, and alcoholic beverages. The berries can also be consumed whole and are employed in various applications in traditional Chinese medicine, as well as in traditional Korean, Japanese, and Tibetan medicine. Additionally, Lycium species serve as food plants for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species, such as Coleophora vigilis, which has been recorded feeding on Lycium ferocissimum.
